evidence.claim: Steens is a fault-block mountain, its eastern edge pushed upward along a fault. From the east rim overlook, the mountain drops more than a vertical mile to the Alvord Desert floor.
evidence.quote: Steens Mountain is an example of a fault-block mountain, formed when massive internal pressure forced the east edge upward along a fault line. From the east rim overlook, the Steens Mountain drops over a vertical mile to the Alvord Desert floor.

evidence.claim: The upper mountain’s meadows once drew cattlemen and Irish and Basque sheepherders for summer grazing.
evidence.quote: Cattlemen, as well as Irish and Basque sheepherders, were once drawn to the upper mountain in the summer to graze their stock on the lush meadows that thrive there.

evidence.claim: At Whorehouse Meadow, aspen carvings left by Basque American sheepherders remain, while the maps record a later dispute: the Bureau of Land Management replaced the name with Naughty Girl Meadow in the 1960s, then restored it in 1981 after public outcry.
evidence.quote: Many of the sheepherders were Basque American immigrants, and their sometimes explicit carvings can still be found in the bark of aspen trees surrounding the meadow. The name was changed in the 1960s to "Naughty Girl Meadow" on Bureau of Land Management maps, but in 1981 the old name was restored after public outcry.

evidence.quote: Sagebrush dominates in the lower, drier environs, giving way to dense stands of juniper, then quaking aspen and mountain mahogany as the moisture levels increase.

evidence.claim: The loop finishes through the range of the South Steens Wild Horse Herd, managed by the Bureau of Land Management.
evidence.quote: The end of the tour loop winds through wild horse country. The South Steens Wild Horse Herd descended from mustangs that escaped from early explorers, Indians, settlers, miners, and ranchers. The herd is managed by the Bureau of Land Management

evidence.claim: Frenchglen takes its name from the French-Glenn Livestock Company, whose headquarters were established here in 1872.
evidence.quote: The community is named after the French-Glenn Livestock Company, founded by Hugh J. Glenn and later joined by his son-in-law, Peter French. French-Glenn built its headquarters there in 1872.

evidence.claim: The post office adopted the name after moving here.
evidence.quote: The post office took the name Frenchglen after it was moved there.

evidence.claim: Its early guests had business at P Ranch or came to visit Malheur National Wildlife Refuge.
evidence.quote: In its early days, its guests typically had business at Peter French's P Ranch or were visiting the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge.

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps labor helped restore and enlarge the hotel in 1937–38; Oregon’s parks department took possession in 1973.
evidence.quote: From 1937 to 1938, the hotel was restored and enlarged by the U.S. Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, with labor from the Civilian Conservation Corps.

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps labor helped restore and enlarge the hotel in 1937–38; Oregon’s parks department took possession in 1973.
evidence.quote: The Oregon Parks and Recreation Department took possession of the property in 1973.

evidence.claim: The historic building has eight guest rooms, with additional accommodation in the modern Drovers’ Inn. Guests continue to visit for the refuge and Steens Mountain.
evidence.quote: Today, the historic hotel building has eight guest rooms, and an additional modern building, the Drovers' Inn, accommodates overflow guests. It also has a dining room. Guests still visit for the wildlife refuge, as well as nearby Steens Mountain.

evidence.claim: Aspens surrounding Whorehouse Meadow retain carvings made by Basque American sheepherders, some of them explicit.

evidence.claim: The meadow lies on Steens Mountain’s western slope within the Steens Mountain Wilderness.
evidence.quote: Whorehouse Meadow is a meadow located on the western slope of Steens Mountain southeast of Frenchglen, Oregon, United States. It lies within the Steens Mountain Wilderness.

evidence.claim: Women from Vale once set up wood-and-canvas tents here to serve the area’s sheepherders and cattlemen.
evidence.quote: Entrepreneuring women from Vale, Oregon, would set up wood and canvas tents in the meadow to provide services to the sheepherders and cattlemen of the area.
